initial_requirements: Tarrant County needs an integrated justice capability to improve the administration of indigent defense services and information sharing across the criminal justice community. The system should help the Office of Attorney Appointments receive and process requests for appointed counsel, obtain relevant defendant and case information, coordinate attorney appointments, and notify the people and justice organizations involved in each request.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What are the primary outcomes Tarrant County wants this integrated justice capability to achieve for indigent defense services, and how will success be measured?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
The main outcome is to make appointed-counsel processing faster, more consistent, and less manual so the Office of Attorney Appointments can handle requests with better information and fewer delays. We also want smoother coordination across the criminal justice community, with timely notifications and better sharing of defendant and case details so appointments are made accurately.
Success would probably be measured by reduced turnaround time from request to appointment, fewer data entry errors or missing information, and fewer follow-up calls or emails to chase down case details. We’d also look at whether users can see the status of a request more easily and whether notifications are getting the right people at the right time, but the exact metrics would still need to be defined with the team.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Which stakeholder groups or user roles will interact with this integrated justice capability, and what responsibilities or permissions should each role have?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
The main users will be staff in the Office of Attorney Appointments, since they’ll be receiving and processing the requests and coordinating the appointment workflow. We’ll also have judges or court staff submitting or initiating requests, and attorneys who may need appointment information and notifications. On the justice-system side, there will likely be jail, clerk, prosecutor, and maybe public defender or other court-connected staff who provide or consume case information, though the exact role permissions still need to be worked out.
In general, Office staff should be able to review cases, verify eligibility information, assign or route appointments, and send notifications. Court users should probably be able to create or submit requests and see status updates relevant to their cases, while attorneys should receive appointment details and updates but not edit case records. Other agencies would likely have more limited access, mostly to share or view the specific information they’re responsible for.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What are the key business rules that should govern how appointed-counsel requests are reviewed, prioritized, approved or rejected, assigned to attorneys, and routed for notifications—for example, eligibility checks, exceptions, deadlines, or criteria that determine who can act on a request and when?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
A request should not move forward until the core defendant and case information is complete enough to make a decision, and the office needs to be able to verify that the person actually qualifies for appointed counsel under county rules. If something is missing or the case is in an exception category, staff should be able to hold it, reject it, or route it for manual review instead of forcing an automatic approval.
Priority would usually depend on case type, court requirements, and any deadlines already attached to the matter, so urgent hearings or expiring timelines should surface first. Only authorized Office of Attorney Appointments staff should approve or assign counsel, while courts may initiate requests and other agencies may provide supporting information but not make the appointment decision. Notifications should go out when a request is received, when it is approved or rejected, when counsel is assigned, and when something changes that affects the parties involved, but I’d want to verify the exact trigger points and exception handling with the team.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What specific types of requests or case situations should be treated as exception categories, and for each one, what should the system do—such as hold, reject, or route to manual review?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
The most obvious exceptions would be requests with missing identity or case details, duplicate requests, conflicts of interest, or situations where the person is clearly not eligible based on the information available. Those should usually be held or routed to manual review rather than automatically approved, because staff need a chance to verify what’s wrong and correct it if possible.
We’d also treat special case types, like emergencies, late-night or same-day requests, and maybe cases involving minors, detention status changes, or unusual court orders, as manual-review items if they don’t fit the normal workflow. If the issue is a hard disqualifier, then rejection makes sense; if it’s just incomplete or ambiguous, holding the request and sending it to the right staff is better. The exact exception list and action for each one would still need to be defined with the office and the courts.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Can you describe how approval authority should be structured for appointed-counsel requests—for example, which specific roles or levels within the Office of Attorney Appointments can approve, assign, override, or manually review requests, and whether any approval rules vary by case type, court, urgency, or exception category?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
In general, I’d expect frontline appointment staff to handle intake, review completeness, and prepare the request, but not necessarily have authority to override a rule or make a final exception decision on their own. Supervisors or designated lead staff should probably be the ones who can approve exceptions, override routing, or manually assign counsel when the normal workflow doesn’t fit.
I would expect some approval rules to vary by case type and urgency, especially for emergency appointments or special categories that need faster handling. Court-specific rules may also matter if a particular court requires certain review steps before assignment, and any exception category that touches eligibility or conflicts should likely require higher-level review. The exact approval matrix isn’t fully defined yet, so we’d need to confirm which roles get which permissions and where the cutoff points are.

turns.interviewer_utterance: For the agencies that will share or consume case information, what data-sharing rules should govern what each agency can see, provide, or update—for example, should access vary by agency type, case type, specific field, or record status, and are there any information-sharing restrictions or approval steps we need to account for?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
Yes, access will definitely need to vary by agency type, and in some cases by case type or by the status of the record. For example, a court or clerk user might need broader visibility into case and appointment status, while a jail or prosecutor user should only see the fields they need to support the process, and updates should be limited to the information that agency is responsible for.
We also need to account for restricted data, like confidential defendant information, sealed matters, or notes that are only visible to office staff or supervisors. Some updates may need approval or validation before they become part of the official record, especially if they affect eligibility, counsel assignment, or court deadlines. I don’t know yet whether there are formal county data-sharing agreements or statutory restrictions that will drive the final rules, so that would need to be confirmed.

slots.value: Office of Attorney Appointments staff, including frontline intake/review staff and supervisors or designated lead staff; judges or court staff who submit or initiate requests; attorneys who receive appointment information and notifications; jail, clerk, prosecutor, and possibly public defender or other court-connected staff who provide or consume case information. Frontline staff may handle intake and completeness review, but supervisors or designated lead staff should handle exceptions, overrides, or manual assignment when the normal workflow does not fit. Supervisors or designated lead staff handle exception approval, overrides, routing, or manual assignment.

Office-only or supervisor-only notes, confidential defendant information, and sealed matters must be restricted. Users may update only the specific information their agency is responsible for.

slots.name: agency_specific_permissions
slots.value: Courts or court staff may create or initiate requests and view relevant status updates. Clerks may have broader visibility into case and appointment status. Jail and prosecutor users should have limited access to the fields they need to support the process and may update only information they are responsible for. Attorneys can receive appointment details and notifications but cannot edit case records. Office staff can review, verify eligibility, assign or route appointments, and send notifications, while supervisors or designated leads can handle exceptions, overrides, and manual assignments.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The stakeholder emphasized that exact notification trigger points and exception handling are still unknown, and that requests may need to be held, rejected, or routed for manual review instead of flowing straight through.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This suggests the county likely has nuanced legal and operational edge cases in indigent-defense processing, where premature or incorrect automated action could create compliance risk, missed deadlines, or improper counsel assignment. The team may need configurable workflow control and auditability before they can trust automation.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The stakeholder mentioned that exact success metrics, exact role permissions, and especially the exception list, trigger points, and handling rules are still not defined and must be worked out with the office and courts.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This likely indicates the county is early in workflow design and may need a configurable case-management solution rather than a fixed one, because local court practices, legal edge cases, and approval responsibilities can vary by court or case type. They may be trying to preserve flexibility, policy alignment, and auditability before locking down automation behavior.

abduction_history.surprising_fact: The stakeholder called out that other agencies will share or consume case information, but their exact role permissions are still unresolved, suggesting the system must accommodate inter-agency data exchange without exposing unnecessary information.
abduction_history.suspected_reason: This likely means the county expects a multi-agency justice environment with sensitive records and varying legal access boundaries, so the system may need fine-grained data segmentation, least-privilege access, and possibly configurable sharing rules by agency, case type, or record field.
